tagline: The great prophet of God's holiness, judgment, and comfort, whose vision runs from the sins of Jerusalem to a new heavens and a new earth.
overview:
Isaiah is the longest and, for many readers, the grandest of the prophetic books. It opens in the eighth century BC with a prophet named Isaiah son of Amoz, who spoke to the kings of Judah while the Assyrian empire swallowed the small nations around them. He saw the Lord enthroned in the temple, heard the seraphim cry that God is holy, and spent his life calling a compromised people back to trust in that holy God rather than in armies, alliances, and idols. The first half of the book is full of judgment on Judah, on the northern kingdom of Israel, and on the nations, but it is threaded with promises: a child named Immanuel, a king on David's throne whose names include Mighty God and Prince of Peace, a shoot from the stump of Jesse, and a mountain where the nations will learn peace.

From chapter 40 the tone and the horizon change. The voice speaks comfort to a people in exile in Babylon, names the Persian king Cyrus as the Lord's instrument of their release, mocks the idols of Babylon, and introduces the mysterious Servant of the Lord who suffers, dies, and is vindicated for the sins of others. The last chapters speak to a community back in the land but still waiting, torn between the faithful and the hypocritical, and they close with a vision of new heavens and a new earth.

Isaiah matters because it holds together what people tend to pull apart: God's fearful holiness and his tender comfort, judgment and hope, Israel's particular calling and the whole world's future. The New Testament quotes it more than almost any other Old Testament book, and the first Christians found in its Servant and its promised king the clearest pictures of Jesus.
author:
The book names its prophet as Isaiah son of Amoz (1:1), who worked in Jerusalem during the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah. He was married to a woman he calls the prophetess and had at least two sons whose names were themselves messages (7:3; 8:3). He had direct access to kings, and the narratives of chapters 36 to 39 show him advising Hezekiah during the Assyrian crisis. A later Jewish tradition holds that he was martyred under Manasseh, but the Bible itself does not say how he died.

Who wrote the whole book is one of the most discussed questions in Old Testament study, and there are three main positions. The traditional view, held by Jewish and Christian readers for most of history and still defended by many evangelical scholars (for example J. Alec Motyer and John Oswalt), is that Isaiah himself is responsible for all sixty-six chapters, and that chapters 40 to 66 are genuine prediction of the exile and return given more than a century and a half in advance. Its defenders point to the New Testament, which quotes both halves under Isaiah's name (John 12:38-41 cites 53:1 and 6:10 together), to the title the Holy One of Israel, which runs through both halves and is rare elsewhere, and to the Great Isaiah Scroll from Qumran, which presents all sixty-six chapters as one book.

Most critical scholars since the late eighteenth century have instead distinguished two or three bodies of material. Chapters 1 to 39 are largely tied to the eighth-century prophet; chapters 40 to 55 (often called Second Isaiah or Deutero-Isaiah) address the exiles in Babylon in the sixth century and assume Jerusalem already lies in ruins; and chapters 56 to 66 (Third Isaiah, a division proposed by Bernhard Duhm in 1892) address the community after the return. They argue from the shift in historical setting, the naming of Cyrus as a present figure, and differences of style and theme. Between these positions stand mediating views: that Isaiah's disciples (compare 8:16) carried on and extended his teaching, or that the book grew over time yet was deliberately shaped as one work, so that its final form should be read as a unity whatever its history. Many scholars now take this canonical approach, reading the book whole while still discussing its layers. On every view, the church confesses that the book as received is God's word.
date:
Isaiah's own ministry can be dated with some confidence. It began around the year King Uzziah died (6:1), usually placed about 740 BC, and ran at least until Sennacherib's invasion of Judah in 701 BC, a span of some forty years. Chapters 1 to 39 largely reflect this period: the war waged on Judah by Aram and Israel around 735 BC, the fall of Samaria in 722 BC, and the Assyrian crisis under Hezekiah.

The date of the book as a whole depends on the authorship question. On the traditional view, it was substantially complete in the early seventh century BC, with chapters 40 to 66 looking ahead to events still to come. On the multiple-author view, chapters 40 to 55 come from the later years of the Babylonian exile, around 550 to 539 BC, shortly before Cyrus took Babylon, and chapters 56 to 66 from the decades after the return, in the late sixth or early fifth century BC. Mediating views place the final shaping of the book in the Persian period while holding that much of its material, and its central vision, go back to Isaiah himself. The Great Isaiah Scroll from Qumran, copied around the second century BC, shows that the book existed in its present sixty-six-chapter form well before that.
setting:
Isaiah lived in the century when Assyria became the first great empire of the ancient Near East. Tiglath-pileser III (reigned 745 to 727 BC) turned Assyria into a machine of conquest that deported whole populations and reduced kingdoms to paying tribute. Judah, a small hill kingdom ruled from Jerusalem by the descendants of David, was caught among Assyria, Egypt to the south, and its own neighbors. Around 735 BC Rezin king of Aram and Pekah king of Israel attacked Judah to force it into an anti-Assyrian coalition; King Ahaz, against Isaiah's counsel, appealed to Assyria for help (2 Kings 16). Assyria took Damascus in 732 BC and Samaria in 722 BC, ending the northern kingdom. Hezekiah later rebelled against Assyria, and in 701 BC Sennacherib ravaged the cities of Judah and besieged Jerusalem, which was spared (chapters 36 and 37; 2 Kings 18 and 19).

The later chapters assume a different world. Babylon has replaced Assyria, Jerusalem and its temple have been destroyed (587 or 586 BC), and the people are in exile. Cyrus the Persian is rising; he took Babylon in 539 BC and allowed exiles to return in 539/538 BC. The final chapters reflect a small community back in Judah, facing disappointment, divided worship, and questions about who belongs to God's people.
purpose: The book calls God's people to trust the Holy One of Israel alone. To the kings of the eighth century it says: do not trust Assyria, Egypt, or your own schemes; God is your security, and unbelief will end in ruin. To a people in exile it says: your God has not forgotten you, he is the only God, the idols are nothing, and he will bring you home. To a community after the return it says: God wants justice and humble hearts rather than empty ritual, and he is still preparing something greater than anything yet seen. Across all three settings, the book aims to form a remnant, a purified people who will be a light to the nations, and to set their hope on a future king, a suffering Servant, and a renewed creation that only God can bring about.
story: Isaiah belongs to the period of the divided kingdom and its end, the era told in 2 Kings 15 to 25 and 2 Chronicles 26 to 36. His contemporaries include Amos and Hosea in the north and Micah in Judah. Isaiah stands between the promise to David in 2 Samuel 7, which he takes up in his visions of a coming king, and the exile and return told in Ezra and Nehemiah, which his later chapters anticipate and address. Jeremiah and Ezekiel, who follow him, speak into the fall of Jerusalem that Isaiah foresaw. Isaiah's great themes of a new exodus, a servant who bears sin, and a new creation become the vocabulary in which the New Testament explains Jesus and the church, and Revelation's closing vision of a new heaven and a new earth draws directly on Isaiah 65 and 66.
christ: No Old Testament book shaped the first Christians' understanding of Jesus more than Isaiah. Matthew reads the sign of Immanuel (7:14) as fulfilled in Jesus' birth, and the light dawning in Galilee (9:1-2) as fulfilled in his ministry there. The child with the names Wonderful Counselor and Mighty God (9:6-7) and the shoot from the stump of Jesse on whom the Spirit rests (11:1-5) became central texts for Jesus as the promised Son of David. John the Baptist is identified with the voice crying in the wilderness (40:3). Jesus began his public teaching in Nazareth by reading Isaiah 61. Above all, the Servant of the Lord who is pierced for our transgressions and makes many righteous (52:13 to 53:12) is read throughout the New Testament as the clearest foreshadowing of the cross (Acts 8:32-35; 1 Peter 2:22-25). Readers debate how much the original audiences understood of these passages, and Jewish interpreters have often read the Servant as Israel. Christians confess that in Jesus these threads of king, servant, and new creation are gathered into one person.
reading: Isaiah is mostly poetry, and it should be read as poetry: images, parallel lines, sudden shifts of speaker, and rapid movement between judgment and hope. It is also an anthology of oracles, not a continuous narrative, so it helps to notice where one unit ends and another begins and to watch for the historical setting each assumes. Keep the three horizons in view: the prophet's own day, the exile and return, and the far future of God's kingdom. Many promises have a near fulfillment and a fuller one, and the book often speaks of the future in the images of its own world (Zion, Assyria, Egypt). Two common misreadings are worth avoiding: treating the book as a list of predictions detached from its history, and treating it as mere history with no word for later readers. The New Testament reads it both ways at once.

structure.title: Judah on trial and the promised king
structure.summary: Oracles of judgment on Judah and Jerusalem, the call of Isaiah, the crisis of King Ahaz, and promises of Immanuel and a righteous king from David's line, ending in a song of praise.

structure.title: Oracles against the nations
structure.summary: Judgment on Babylon, Assyria, Philistia, Moab, Damascus, Egypt, Tyre, and others. The Lord who judges Judah rules every nation.

structure.title: Judgment and feast for the whole world
structure.summary: Often called the Isaiah apocalypse: the earth laid waste, then a banquet on Zion where God swallows up death and wipes away tears.

structure.title: Woes, false trust, and the coming kingdom
structure.summary: Warnings against trusting Egypt and against Jerusalem's leaders, alternating with visions of a righteous king and the desert blooming as the redeemed return.

structure.title: Hezekiah, Assyria, and Babylon
structure.summary: Narrative of Sennacherib's siege and Jerusalem's deliverance, Hezekiah's illness and recovery, and his display of treasure to Babylonian envoys, which points ahead to exile. These chapters close the first major part of the book, chapters 1 to 39.

structure.title: Comfort for the exiles
structure.summary: The second major part (40 to 55) begins: God comes to bring his people home, proves himself the only God against Babylon's idols, and names Cyrus as his instrument.

structure.title: The Servant and the restoration of Zion
structure.summary: The Servant is called to restore Israel and bring light to the nations, suffers and dies for the sins of many, and Zion is invited to rejoice in an everlasting covenant.

structure.title: The waiting community and the new creation
structure.summary: The third major part addresses the returned community: true worship and justice, confession of sin, the glory of a restored Zion, and new heavens and a new earth.

themes.title: The Holy One of Israel
themes.body: Isaiah's signature title for God appears throughout the book and rarely anywhere else. It comes from the vision of chapter 6, where the seraphim call God holy three times. Holiness in Isaiah means God's utter otherness and moral purity, which exposes human sin and pride, but it also means his commitment to his people: the Holy One is Israel's Holy One, and he is their Redeemer.

themes.title: Trust or ruin
themes.body: Again and again the kings of Judah face a choice between trusting God and trusting military power, foreign alliances, or clever policy. Ahaz chooses Assyria; Hezekiah, in the crisis of 701 BC, prays. The book's verdict is that faith is the only real security, and that everything people lean on in its place, from horses to idols, will fail them.

themes.title: Judgment and the remnant
themes.body: God's judgment in Isaiah is real and severe, but it is not the last word. Through it God preserves a remnant, a purified people who will return to him. The name of Isaiah's son Shear-jashub, a remnant will return, holds both the threat and the hope together.

themes.title: The king, the Servant, and the anointed one
themes.body: Isaiah offers three great portraits of the one through whom God will act: a royal child from David's line who brings justice and peace (chapters 9 and 11), a Servant who suffers for others and brings light to the nations (chapters 42 to 53), and an anointed messenger of good news to the poor (chapter 61). The New Testament sees all three in Jesus.

themes.title: Zion and the nations
themes.body: Jerusalem, or Zion, is the city God judges and the city he will restore. Isaiah sees it becoming the place where all nations come to learn God's ways (2:2-4; 60:1-3), so that the calling of Israel turns out to be for the sake of the whole world.

themes.title: New exodus and new creation
themes.body: The later chapters describe the return from exile as a second exodus, with a road through the wilderness and water in the desert, and they finally reach beyond Israel's history to new heavens and a new earth where weeping is no more (65:17-25).

keyChapters.why: The book's overture: God puts his people on trial, rejects worship without justice, and offers cleansing to those who repent.
Isaiah's vision of the Lord on his throne and his call, the source of the book's vision of God as the Holy One.
King Ahaz refuses to trust God, and Isaiah gives the sign of Immanuel, later read by Matthew as fulfilled in Jesus' birth.
The promise of light for Galilee and a child on David's throne whose names include Wonderful Counselor and Prince of Peace.
Hezekiah prays in the Assyrian crisis and Jerusalem is delivered, the great example of the trust the book calls for.
Comfort for the exiles: a voice in the wilderness, the frailty of flesh, and the everlasting word of God.
The Servant who is despised, pierced, and crushed for the sins of others, then vindicated, the Old Testament passage most closely tied to the cross.
God's promise of new heavens and a new earth, the vision the Bible's final chapters take up.
